title: Lists and Dynamic Sequences
learningObjectives: Explain a list or dynamic sequence as a collection designed to manage a changing number of items.
Describe common operations for appending, inserting, removing, and accessing list elements.
Compare dynamic sequences with fixed-size arrays at a conceptual level.
Recognize that insertion or removal can affect later indexes and element positions.
Choose a dynamic sequence when the number of elements changes during program use.

understand.concept: Lists and dynamic sequences commonly provide a collection that can grow or shrink as items are added or removed. They often support operations such as append, insert, remove, search, and indexed access. Internally, some are array-backed and may resize or shift elements when their size changes.
understand.whyItMatters: Applications rarely know every item in advance. Dynamic sequences let programs manage changing data such as shopping carts, task lists, search results, and messages while using collection operations rather than manual storage.
understand.analogy: A list is like a queue of cards that can be expanded: insert a new card, remove one, or move cards to make space. The positions of later cards may change after an insertion or removal.
understand.analogyLimit: List implementations differ in performance and capabilities. Some have efficient insertion at one end, others at arbitrary positions; the analogy does not imply that every operation costs the same.

explain.narrative: Use a dynamic list when items are added or removed during the program's life. Append is often convenient for adding at the end. Insert and remove may shift later positions, so indexes can change. When frequent insertion at the middle or front is expected, consider the collection implementation's performance or a different structure. Avoid assuming the list's size is fixed or that operations have identical cost.

examples.title: Start an empty list
examples.explanation: An empty dynamic sequence can begin with no items and grow as work is added.

examples.title: Append an item
examples.explanation: Appending adds an item to the end of the list.

examples.title: Insert at a position
examples.explanation: Insertion at index 1 places an item there and shifts later elements in this JavaScript array.

examples.title: Remove an item
examples.explanation: Removing at index 0 shifts later items toward the front; their positions change.

examples.title: Update a changing list
examples.explanation: A list can grow and shrink with operations that change its length.

commonMistakes: Assuming an index remains attached to the same item after insertion or removal.
Using a fixed-size array concept when the task needs changing length.
Ignoring the cost of repeated insertion or removal in certain positions.
Removing an item without checking whether it exists.
Using a list for uniqueness or key lookup when another collection type is more appropriate.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Plan a collection operation
guidedTask.instructions: Use "Lists and Dynamic Sequences" to solve a small data-management task.
steps: Describe the group of data and whether order matters.
Choose the collection type and explain why.
Show an operation that reads or changes the collection.
Trace what happens to size or positions.
Test empty, single-item, and typical cases as appropriate.

independentTask.title: Independent: Manage a changing data group
independentTask.instructions: Build a small collection scenario using your own values and demonstrate the operations.
requirements: Show the resulting size or item positions.
Explain why this collection type fits.

hints: Ask whether order, indexes, uniqueness, or keys matter.
Use the length/size value instead of hard-coding counts.
Insertion and removal can change later positions.
Test an empty collection and one item before larger cases.
